sections.h2: Your options for selling in La Crosse
sections.html:
La Crosse sellers weigh three paths: an agent listing, a private sale, and a cash offer from a buyer who accepts the house in its current condition. About 50,784 people lived in the city on July 1, 2025, down 3.6 percent from the April 2020 base of 52,691.

Timing and condition usually decide it. A listing puts the house in front of the most buyers, among them people who work at the city's large employers and the university. A direct sale suits an owner facing a move, a vacant rental, an estate or repairs they would rather not fund.

La Crosse has far more renters than most Wisconsin cities. Only 46.1 percent of households own their home, so rented housing makes up a large share of the market, and many sellers are investors or heirs. Median age is young, and the college neighborhoods around UW-La Crosse behave differently from the quieter residential blocks.

Employers and campuses drive demand. Mention the nearest large employer or school when you describe the house, since proximity to work is what those households ask about first.

Home values and incomes here run lower than in many Wisconsin cities, while the commute is short. A citywide median is only a guide to a single house.

The mean trip to work is 15.9 minutes, a short commute that is a selling point worth putting in front of a buyer.

La Crosse has 13 voting wards, and its neighborhoods include Bluffside, Washburn, Historic Cass and King, Powell-Poage-Hamilton, Historic Downtown, Northside, Grandview Emerson, Weigent Hogan, Hintgen, College Park and Springbrook Clayton Johnson. College Park is the district around the University of Wisconsin-La Crosse campus. Naming the neighborhood in your listing helps buyers search the way they already think about the city.

Interstate 90, U.S. 14, 53 and 61, and state highways 35, 16 and 33 serve the city, and the Cass Street and Cameron Avenue bridges connect downtown with La Crescent, Minnesota. La Crosse Regional Airport offers scheduled service to Chicago.

sections.h2: Rental rules that affect a La Crosse house
sections.html:
La Crosse regulates both long-term and short-term rentals, so an investor selling a rental house should know which rules apply. Residential rental units are registered with the Building and Inspections office in the Planning and Development Department, and the application charges $10 for each parcel (email inspection@cityoflacrosse.org or call 608-789-7530). Ask the office whether the registration stays with the owner or must be redone by the buyer.

Short-term rentals fall under Article XIX of the city code. The ordinance defines them as a residential dwelling rented for a fee for fewer than 30 consecutive days, and the City Clerk issues the license. A short-term rental license cannot be transferred to a buyer, and no advertisement may run until the required county, state and local permits are in hand. A buyer who plans to run the house as a short-term rental therefore has to apply on their own.

  • Registration of a rental unit: Building and Inspections.
  • Short-term rental license: City Clerk, under Article XIX.
  • Tax account questions: La Crosse County Treasurer, 212 6th Street North, (608) 785-9711, open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays.

The seller owes Wisconsin's transfer fee of 30 cents for each $100 of value or fraction thereof (Wis. Stat. 77.22). The county register of deeds collects it at recording. The grantor and the grantee sign the electronic return, and the register cannot record the deed without it.

Some transfers are free of the fee, including transfers by will or descent and transfers between a parent and child for nominal consideration (Wis. Stat. 77.25). Plan for these steps:

  • Order title work and a payoff letter for any mortgage.
  • File the transfer return with the Department of Revenue and keep the receipt.
  • Record the deed at the La Crosse County Register of Deeds.
  • Settle prorated taxes at closing.

An owner of a property with one to four dwelling units delivers a completed Real Estate Condition Report within 10 days after the buyer's contract is accepted. If the report is late, the buyer has two business days after the tenth day to rescind and recover any deposit (Wis. Stat. 709.02). Executors and trustees who never lived in the house are excused.

Real estate tax is payable on or before January 31 and July 31 in two equal parts, unless the total bill is under $100 (Wis. Stat. 74.11). Delinquent amounts are paid to the county treasurer with interest and penalties charged from the preceding February 1. The next date is January 31, 2027, so ask the treasurer for the current balance before you set a closing date.

faqs.q: How long does it take to sell a house in La Crosse?
faqs.a: It depends on the route. A listing moves at the pace of showings, inspection and lender approval, while a direct sale can close as soon as the title work and the transfer return are done. Ask your title company to estimate the schedule after you have a signed contract.

faqs.q: Do I need a license to sell a La Crosse rental house?
faqs.a: Rental units are registered with the Building and Inspections office, which charges $10 per parcel on its application. Short-term rental licenses come from the City Clerk and cannot be transferred, so a buyer applies on their own.

faqs.q: What does the transfer fee cost in La Crosse?
faqs.a: It is 30 cents per $100 of value or fraction thereof, charged to the seller and collected by the county register of deeds when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in La Crosse?
faqs.a: Payments made on or before January 31 go to the local taxation district treasurer and later payments go to the county treasurer. The La Crosse County Treasurer is at 212 6th Street North and can be reached at (608) 785-9711.

faqs.q: Can an estate sell a La Crosse house without a condition report?
faqs.a: A personal representative, trustee or court-appointed fiduciary who has never occupied the house is excused from the report under chapter 709. The sale still needs a deed, a transfer return and any exemption language the register requires.
